The histogram shows the Saccharide P@10 distribution of representative 15-gene windows across 556 evaluable viral loci, with colours indicating selection evidence pooled across both window sizes. A total of 287 loci met at least one selection criterion.

B. Taxonomic distribution of 242 viral genomes containing putative glycan-associated GT neighbourhoods, identified by BGC-Prophet Saccharide classification and/or embedding-based retrieval (≥5 Saccharide-annotated BGCs among the ten nearest MIBiG references; P@10 ≥ 0.5)

Uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) of BGC-Prophet embeddings, showing MIBiG reference BGCs and selected viral GT-associated loci. Left, saccharide-associated reference BGCs (n = 195) are coloured according to their annotated chemotypes: capsule, extracellular polysaccharide (EPS)/matrix polysaccharide, lipopolysaccharide/lipooligosaccharide/O-antigen (LPS/LOS), S-layer/other surface glycan, aminoglycoside/aminocyclitol, glycosylated specialized metabolite, and other/unresolved. The remaining reference BGCs (n = 2,307) are shown in light grey, with viral loci indicated by pale triangles. Right, 287 selected viral GT-associated loci are coloured according to five communities identified by exploratory Leiden clustering: VC01 (n = 68), VC02 (n = 55), VC03 (n = 74), VC04 (n = 35) and VC05 (n = 55). Saccharide-associated reference BGCs are shown as gold circles, and other reference BGCs as a grey background. Both panels use the same UMAP coordinates.

surrounding_text: Protein structures from the C005 (13 proteins) and C009 (15 proteins) network reference sets were analysed alongside R699 (Protein Data Bank accession 9DYT, chain A). Reference structures were compared all against all using Foldseek, and each community medoid was selected as the structure with the highest median symmetric TM-score against other members. Separate reference-only structural alignments were generated using FoldMason. Reference cores comprised medoid residues passing the within-community quality filter, with a within-community local structural similarity score ≥0.75 and residue presence ≥0.70. Cores were defined without R699 and held fixed during projection. Each reference set was then realigned with R699, and core positions were transferred through the medoid’s ungapped residue indices to corresponding R699 alignment positions. Individual R699 residues were classified as mapping to both cores, C005 only, C009 only or neither. Residue classes were mapped to chain-A coordinate numbering and visualized in PyMOL. Here, support denotes alignment correspondence to a reference core.
Supplementary Figures & Methods
Supplementary Figure 1. Structural clustering of viral GT candidates.

The 1,081 viral proteins assigned to 115 multi-member clusters are shown as nodes, with each connected component representing one final Foldseek cluster. Blue nodes denote the 115 final cluster representatives, orange nodes denote 620 direct members with an explicit non-self representative–member alignment in the Foldseek m8 output, and purple nodes denote 346 indirect members assigned to the same final cluster but lacking an explicit alignment to the final representative in the current alignment output. Solid edges represent explicit representative–member alignments, whereas dashed edges were for indirect members and do not represent additional pairwise structural alignments. The dominant cluster contained 594 proteins. The 646 singleton proteins are not shown. Node positions and edge lengths reflect the Cytoscape layout.

Supplementary Figure 2. Positive-control spike-in benchmark of permissive Foldseek coarse clustering. A. Foldseek clustering of 1,727 viral GT candidates produced 761 clusters, including a dominant cluster of 594 proteins represented by A0A3Q8Q3U2. After adding seven structural entries representing six viral GT controls, clustering with unchanged parameters recovered all seven entries in the cluster represented by A0A3Q8Q3U2. The resulting cluster contained 483 entries, comprising 439 original dominant-cluster members, 37 proteins from other clusters and seven controls. Two nanobody chains co-deposited with CvHAS (PDB 7SP6) were excluded.

B. Structural superposition (left) and indidividual structures (right) of the six viral GT controls: A197 from Sulfolobus turreted icosahedral virus 1 (green; PDB 2C0N); Chlorella virus hyaluronan synthase (CvHAS) from Paramecium bursaria Chlorella virus CZ-2 (cyan; PDB 7SP6, chain A); the virion glycosylation-associated glycosyltransferase gp110 from Mycobacterium phage Che8 (magenta; AlphaFold 3 model); the multidomain glycosyltransferase A111/114R from Paramecium bursaria Chlorella virus 1 (yellow; UniProt Q84432; full-length AlphaFold 3 model); the multidomain rhamnosyltransferase/methyltransferase A064R from Paramecium bursaria Chlorella virus 1 (salmon; full-length AlphaFold 3 model); and the bifunctional lysyl hydroxylase/glycosyltransferase L230 from Acanthamoeba polyphaga mimivirus (purple; UniProt Q5UQC3; full-length AlphaFold 3 models).

surrounding_text: Supplementary Figure 3. Distribution and structural assessment of viral GT candidate clusters.

a. Exact size distribution of the 115 multi-member clusters containing 1,081 proteins. The 43-member and dominant 594-member clusters are highlighted. The median cluster size was 2 proteins (IQR, 2–4).b. Distribution of cluster-level median protein lengths across cluster-size classes. Each point represents one cluster; boxes show the IQR, centre lines the median, whiskers 1.5 × IQR and diamonds the arithmetic mean. The 594-member cluster is shown as a single point.c. Fractions of short (≤102 amino acids) and long (≥763 amino acids) proteins across cluster-size classes. Values indicate outlier counts relative to the total number of proteins in each class.d. Pairwise structural comparisons of 383 protein pairs from 63 smaller clusters lacking direct representative–member alignments in the initial Foldseek output. Axes show the minimum query/target coverage, min(qcov, tcov), and minimum query/target-normalized TM-score, min(qTM, tTM); colour indicates LDDT. Comparisons from the 20-member A0A6J5N5Z7 cluster are shown as circles and all others as triangles. Dashed lines indicate thresholds of 0.50.

e. Supported-pair density for the same 63 clusters, defined as the fraction of all possible within-cluster pairs satisfying both min(qTM, tTM) ≥ 0.50 and min(qcov, tcov) ≥ 0.50. Coincident observations are shown as stacked dots; A0A6J5N5Z7 is highlighted.f. Representative-level Foldseek assignments for all 114 non-giant clusters. Four representatives were classified as GT-like, 23 as non-GT and 87 as ambiguous or unresolved.

surrounding_text: c. Cliff’s δ comparing singleton proteins with proteins from other non-giant multi-member clusters. Points show Cliff’s δ and horizontal bars indicate 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Negative values indicate lower values among singletons. Effect sizes were −0.661 for protein length (95% CI, −0.708 to −0.621), −0.224 for median pLDDT (95% CI, −0.288 to −0.161) and 0.281 for the fraction of residues with pLDDT below 70 (95% CI, 0.216 to 0.340). Statistical comparisons used two-sided Mann–Whitney U tests with Benjamini–Hochberg correction (adjusted P = 1.24 × 10⁻⁸⁰, 1.17 × 10⁻¹⁰ and 5.80 × 10⁻¹⁶, respectively).

D. Grouping of 646 singleton proteins by structure-represented length (122 aa threshold) and median pLDDT (70 threshold). Of these, 328 (50.8%) were shorter than 122 aa with median pLDDT below 70, whereas 93 (14.4%) had lengths of at least 122 aa and median pLDDT of at least 70.
Supplementary Figure 5.  Multi-protein structural communities substantially recapitulate CAZy family-level organization.

A. Community-level CAZy purity. The 80 multi-protein structural communities (4,274 proteins) were classified according to the proportion of CAZy-annotated members belonging to the most abundant family within each community. Communities containing at least three unambiguously annotated proteins were classified as family-coherent (purity ≥0.80; 32 communities) or mixed (purity <0.80; 6 communities). The remaining 42 communities were designated annotation-limited. The upper bar shows the number of communities in each category; the lower bar shows the corresponding protein counts, including proteins without CAZy assignments.

B. CAZy family concentration. For each of 39 CAZy families, concentration was defined as the fraction of its annotated members found in the structural community containing the largest number of members of that family. Thirty-three families (84.6%) had a concentration of at least 0.80 (upper bar). Across 3,968 unambiguously CAZy-annotated proteins, 3,543 (89.3%) occurred in their respective family's largest community, whereas 425 (10.7%) were distributed elsewhere (lower bar). The 580 singleton proteins were excluded from both analyses. CAZy annotations were applied after structural community detection and did not influence community assignment.

Supplementary Figure 6.  Distinct structural relationships of viral glycosyltransferases within the GT-A landscape.

A. Structural placement of CAZy-unassigned viral GTs (F2YIU4 and G8DH22) within the GT31 family. Local structure-similarity network showing GT31 reference proteins coloured by functional subgroup, as indicated in the key. CAZy-unassigned viral proteins F2Y1U4 and G8DH22 are shown as purple diamonds, with F2Y1U4 highlighted by a dashed red circle. Structural comparison of the GT31 reference Q18515 and F2Y1U4 shows the strict pan-GT31 core (dark teal), additional structurally supported positions (light blue) and non-core regions (grey). Bars summarize structural comparisons of F2Y1U4 across four GT31 reference subclusters, showing mean subcluster-median sequence identity (16.42%), query coverage (99.25%) and alignment TM-score (AlnTM, 0.7996).

B. Domain-specific structural relationships of R699 across communities C005 and C009. Local structure-similarity network highlighting C005 (orange), C009 (turquoise), R699 (purple diamond) and the PLOD-like glycosyltransferase Q20679 (purple oval); remaining proteins are shown in grey. Upper, sequence identities between R699 and Q20679 mapped onto the R699 structure following FoldMason alignment. Identical residues are shown in teal, identical active-site residues in magenta, and non-identical active-site residues in orange. Other residues are shown in grey. Lower, conserved structural cores independently defined from C005 and C009 reference proteins mapped onto R699. Both communities showed extensive structural correspondence within the non-UDP-binding domain, whereas the UDP-binding catalytic domain showed limited structural support.

Structural comparison of the GT31 reference Q18515 and F2Y1U4 shows the strict pan-GT31 core (dark teal), additional structurally supported positions (light blue) and non-core regions (grey). Bars summarize structural comparisons of F2Y1U4 across four GT31 reference subclusters, showing mean subcluster-median sequence identity (16.42%), query coverage (99.25%) and alignment TM-score (AlnTM, 0.7996).

B. Domain-specific structural relationships of R699 across communities C005 and C009. Local structure-similarity network highlighting C005 (orange), C009 (turquoise), R699 (purple diamond) and the PLOD-like glycosyltransferase Q20679 (purple oval); remaining proteins are shown in grey. Upper, sequence identities between R699 and Q20679 mapped onto the R699 structure following FoldMason alignment. Identical residues are shown in teal, identical active-site residues in magenta, and non-identical active-site residues in orange. Other residues are shown in grey. Lower, conserved structural cores independently defined from C005 and C009 reference proteins mapped onto R699. Both communities showed extensive structural correspondence within the non-UDP-binding domain, whereas the UDP-binding catalytic domain showed limited structural support.

surrounding_text: Supplementary Figure 9. Iterative structural clustering identifies cluster 8 as a dark viral GT subnetwork.Structure similarity network of viral glycosyltransferase candidates generated from all-vs-all structural comparison. Nodes represent predicted viral GT-like proteins and edges represent pairwise structural similarity above the selected threshold. Iterative refinement of the initial clustering result revealed a small, distinct subnetwork, designated cluster 8 (red box). Cluster 8 was separated from the major viral GT communities and was prioritized for further analysis because its members lacked confident conventional sequence-based annotation but retained GT-like structural features and were subsequently found in DNA-modification-associated gene neighborhoods.

Supplementary Fig. 14. Structure-guided annotation of Type II TET/JBP-like oxygenases supports a thymine/5-methyluracil hydroxylation module.Predicted Type II oxygenases encoded in DNA-associated cluster 8 loci were compared with structurally characterized TET/JBP-like 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases. The left panel shows structural superposition of Type II oxygenases with reference Naegleria gruberi TET-like dioxygenase 1 and human TET-family oxygenase structures. The right panels show active-site comparisons centered on the catalytic metal, 2-oxoglutarate-binding region, and flipped-base recognition pocket. Residues involved in Fe(II) coordination are highlighted in blue, whereas residues involved in 2-oxoglutarate binding are highlighted in magenta. These catalytic features are spatially conserved across the Type II oxygenases and reference enzymes, supporting annotation of the Type II proteins as TET/JBP-like 2OG/Fe(II) dioxygenases. The flipped-base recognition pocket is also conserved, including spatially aligned aromatic residues positioned to stack against or stabilize the extruded pyrimidine base. Notably, both Type II oxygenases contain an Asp-to-Asn substitution at the base-recognition position corresponding to the cytosine/5mC-specific Asp in TET-like enzymes. This substitution is consistent with a shift toward thymine/5-methyluracil recognition and supports a model in which the Type II oxygenases generate 5-hydroxymethyluracil-like DNA bases for downstream glycosylation by neighboring cluster 8 GTs.

surrounding_text: Supplementary Fig. 13. Structure-guided annotation of hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor enzymes in DNA-associated cluster 8 loci.Structural and active-site comparison of predicted folate-dependent pyrimidine C5-hydroxymethyltransferases encoded near DNA-associated cluster 8 loci. The top panel shows structural superposition of representative cluster 3-neighborhood enzymes with the crystallographic reference T4 deoxycytidylate 5-hydroxymethyltransferase. The reference structure contains bound tetrahydrofolate (THF) and deoxycytidylate/dCMP-site ligand, providing an active-site template for substrate-recognition analysis. Predicted enzymes from Type I and Type IV loci, including AKJ73159, QFP95377, and QWS69716, preserve the cytosine-directed active-site architecture of T4-like dCMP hydroxymethyltransferases, including the catalytic cysteine, conserved histidine/serine residues, aromatic base-positioning residue, and an Asp residue positioned for cytosine recognition. These features support annotation of these proteins as dCMP C5-hydroxymethyltransferase-like enzymes that can generate 5hmC-type precursors for downstream DNA glycosylation. In contrast, the Type III enzyme BAG41679 preserves the same global fold and catalytic cysteine but contains Asn242 at the position equivalent to the cytosine-specific Asp residue in dCMP-directed enzymes. This Asp-to-Asn active-site substitution is consistent with altered pyrimidine specificity and supports annotation of BAG41679 as a dUMP hydroxymethyltransferase-like enzyme predicted to generate a 5-hydroxymethyluracil-type precursor. Together, these comparisons justify the assignment of Type I/IV loci as 5hmC-linked pathways and the Type III locus as a distinct 5hmdU-linked hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine pathway.

Supplementary Fig. 14. Structure-guided annotation of Type II TET/JBP-like oxygenases supports a thymine/5-methyluracil hydroxylation module.Predicted Type II oxygenases encoded in DNA-associated cluster 8 loci were compared with structurally characterized TET/JBP-like 2-oxoglutarate/Fe(II)-dependent dioxygenases. The left panel shows structural superposition of Type II oxygenases with reference Naegleria gruberi TET-like dioxygenase 1 and human TET-family oxygenase structures. The right panels show active-site comparisons centered on the catalytic metal, 2-oxoglutarate-binding region, and flipped-base recognition pocket. Residues involved in Fe(II) coordination are highlighted in blue, whereas residues involved in 2-oxoglutarate binding are highlighted in magenta. These catalytic features are spatially conserved across the Type II oxygenases and reference enzymes, supporting annotation of the Type II proteins as TET/JBP-like 2OG/Fe(II) dioxygenases. The flipped-base recognition pocket is also conserved, including spatially aligned aromatic residues positioned to stack against or stabilize the extruded pyrimidine base. Notably, both Type II oxygenases contain an Asp-to-Asn substitution at the base-recognition position corresponding to the cytosine/5mC-specific Asp in TET-like enzymes. This substitution is consistent with a shift toward thymine/5-methyluracil recognition and supports a model in which the Type II oxygenases generate 5-hydroxymethyluracil-like DNA bases for downstream glycosylation by neighboring cluster 8 GTs.

surrounding_text: Supplementary Fig. 15. Structural annotation of additional GT-like enzymes in the B2ZYD6 Type III locus.Additional proteins including BAG41682, 41683, 41684, 41685 encoded in the B2ZYD6 Type III locus were compared structurally with E. coli chondroitin synthase, a GT2-fold glycosyltransferase reference. Global structural superposition and active-site inspection show that several B2ZYD6 proteins adopt GT-like folds with conserved nucleotide-sugar donor-binding architecture, supporting their annotation as putative glycosyltransferases which contribute to downstream elaboration of a DNA-linked glycan.

surrounding_text: Supplementary Fig. 15. Structural annotation of additional GT-like enzymes in the B2ZYD6 Type III locus.Additional proteins including BAG41682, 41683, 41684, 41685 encoded in the B2ZYD6 Type III locus were compared structurally with E. coli chondroitin synthase, a GT2-fold glycosyltransferase reference. Global structural superposition and active-site inspection show that several B2ZYD6 proteins adopt GT-like folds with conserved nucleotide-sugar donor-binding architecture, supporting their annotation as putative glycosyltransferases which contribute to downstream elaboration of a DNA-linked glycan.

surrounding_text: Supplementary Fig. 16 .AKJ73146 preserves conserved features of T4-like α-glucosyltransferases.Sequence alignment result between Enterobacteria phage T4 α-glucosyltransferases and  AKJ73146 was mapped onto the predicted AKJ73146 structure. Conserved residues are shown in red and variable residues in blue. The global view (left) shows conservation across the catalytic cleft and DNA-binding surface, while the active-site zoom (right) highlights strong conservation around the predicted catalytic pocket. This pattern supports AKJ73146 as a T4-like α-glucosyltransferase that likely performs the first glucosylation step on 5hmC-DNA.

Supplementary Fig. 17. BAG41686 and AKJ73160 retain electropositive DNA-binding grooves.Electrostatic surface maps of contig 32, BAG41686, and AKJ73160 modeled with modified DNA acceptors. Blue indicates electropositive surface potential and red indicates electronegative potential. The reference DNA GT contig 32 contains a positively charged groove that accommodates the DNA phosphate backbone. BAG41686 preserves a comparable groove, supporting direct binding of hydroxymethylated DNA. AKJ73160 also retains an electropositive DNA-binding surface, consistent with DNA-associated substrate recognition, although its active site is remodeled to recognize Glc-5hmC rather than naked 5hmC. These results support distinct acceptor-recognition modes within a shared DNA-binding framework.

cluster8_relevant_text.text: Cluster 8 formed another compact six-protein module within C001 (Figure. 2c,d), but its genomic neighbourhoods pointed to different biosynthetic contexts. Some members occurred alongside hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine and DNA-modification enzymes, whereas others were associated with virion structural and glycan-related genes (Figure. 4). This suggests that structurally related viral GTs may participate in distinct glycosylation pathways. We therefore focused on the DNA-associated loci, where neighbouring enzymes provided a chemical basis for investigating glycosylation of modified viral DNA.

Within the viral GT structure-similarity network, Cluster 8 emerged as a coherent group of CAZy-unassigned viral proteins (Supplementary Figure. 9). Despite substantial sequence divergence, Cluster 8 members retained high structural similarity (Supplementary Figure. 11) and shared a conserved GT-A-like structural core (Figure. 3A,B). Sequence- and structure-based conservation analyses further revealed that the central scaffold was preserved, whereas peripheral regions were more variable, particularly surface-exposed loops (Figure. 3D,E). Together, these findings support Cluster 8 as a structurally coherent, previously uncharacterized viral GT-like lineage.

Next,  we analyzed whether cluster 8  members shared a conserved genomic context, we extracted local gene neighborhoods around each cluster 8 member and compared their gene neighborhoods (Figure 4). Neighboring genes were classified by predicted functions in hydroxymethyl-base precursor formation, pyrimidine/nucleotide metabolism, DNA metabolism, glycan biosynthesis and virion structure, along with uncharacterized ORFs. This comparison revealed at least two distinct genomic contexts rather than a single conserved gene organization.

In one subset, Cluster 8-containing gene neighborhoods showed disntict combinations of DNA-modification, glycan-biosynthetic and virion-associated genes. This contained predicted dCMP/dUMP hydroxymethylase-like enzymes and other hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine-associated functions, together with DNA-metabolism genes and additional GT-like proteins. These associations suggest a potential role in viral DNA glycosylation, with hydroxymethylated pyrimidines serving as candidate glycosyl acceptors.

In contrast, other Cluster 8-containing loci lacked comparable hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor signatures but were associated with glycan-related enzymes and virion structural genes, including capsid, portal and tail proteins. This distinct genomic organization suggests a potential association with virion glycosylation rather than DNA modification, although the identity of the acceptor substrates remains unexplored. Thus, despite their shared structural architecture, Cluster 8 proteins occur in different glycosylation-associated genomic environments, raising the possibility that this divergent lineage participates in distinct viral biosynthetic processes. We therefore focused subsequent mechanistic analysis on the DNA-associated subset, where the accompanying precursor enzymes provide a chemical basis for investigating putative DNA-glycosylation pathways.

Comparative analysis of DNA-modification-associated Cluster 8 loci identified an unusual glycan-biosynthetic module in jumbo phage B2ZYD6 (Figure. 5). The Type III locus encodes five tandem GT-like proteins (BAG41682–BAG41686), a putative hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor enzyme, and sulfation-associated proteins (BAG41681 and BAG41687). In contrast to canonical T4-like DNA-glucosylation systems, this combination suggests the capacity to assemble an extended DNA-linked glycan and further modify it through sulfation. One possible product is a sulfated pentasaccharide attached to a hydroxymethylated pyrimidine. Sulfated N-glycans have previously been identified on viral envelope glycoproteins (Shilatifard et al., 1993; Karaivanova and Spiro, 1998), but sulfation of DNA-linked glycans in bacteriophages has not, to our knowledge, been demonstrated. Such chemical elaboration could alter how bacterial defence systems recognize modified phage DNA, potentially contributing to the ongoing host–phage evolutionary conflict.

The Type IV locus, by contrast, contained a Cluster 8 GT alongside an α-glucosyltransferase-like enzyme related to characterized T4 enzymes that install the first glucose onto 5hmC-containing DNA ((Sommer et al., 2004; Larivière et al., 2005). This arrangement suggests a possible sequential glycosylation pathway, in which the Cluster 8 enzyme acts downstream of the initial glucosylation step (Figure. 5).

To investigate whether these Cluster 8-associated loci could provide suitable DNA-glycosylation acceptors, we examined their hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor enzymes through structure-guided active-site analysis (Supplementary Figures. 13 and 14). Type I and IV loci encoded dCMP hydroxymethylase-like enzymes retaining the catalytic residues and cytosine-recognition Asp characteristic of dCMP-directed hydroxymethylation, consistent with the formation of 5hmC-type precursors. Type II loci instead contained TET/JBP-like dioxygenases, suggesting a possible post-replicative route to hydroxymethylated pyrimidines. In the Type III locus, BAG41679 retained a folate-dependent pyrimidine C5-hydroxymethylase scaffold but carried Asn242 in place of the Asp residue associated with cytosine recognition, suggesting that BAG41679 uses dUMP rather than d CMP.

To investigate how Cluster 8-associated GTs might catalyse the first and subsequent sugar-transfer steps in DNA glycosylation, we compared the active-site architectures of BAG41686 and AKJ73160 from the Type III and IV loci, respectively, with those of characterized DNA glycosyltransferases (Figure. 6). In the expanded B2ZYD6 Type III locus, BAG41686 retained two key structural elements involved in direct hydroxymethyl-base recognition: the αF helix and Loop X (Figure. 6B). The αF helix contains the predicted catalytic base and an adjacent aromatic residue positioned for π–π stacking with the flipped 5hmU pyrimidine ring (Figure. 6C). This arrangement, also found in characterized first-sugar-installing viral GTs such as contig 32 (Pyle et al., 2024), could position the hydroxymethyl oxygen towards the anomeric carbon of the nucleotide-sugar donor, while the nearby catalytic base facilitates proton abstraction and glycosyl transfer. Loop X further contributes to acceptor positioning through interactions with the DNA deoxyribose. Together, these features support BAG41686 as a candidate first-sugar installer.

In contrast, the Type IV locus encodes AKJ73146, a T4-like α-glucosyltransferase predicted to install the first glucose onto 5hmC-containing DNA (Supplementary Figure. 16), alongside the Cluster 8 enzyme AKJ73160. Unlike BAG41686 and other first-sugar-installing GTs, AKJ73160 lacks the αF-associated aromatic residue involved in direct hydroxymethyl-base recognition (Figure. 6B,D). Instead, the aromatic contact with the underlying 5hmC base is shifted to F151 in Loop X, while Asn174 is positioned near the glucose moiety already attached to 5hmC. This rearrangement of the acceptor-binding pocket could accommodate a pre-glucosylated DNA substrate and orient a hydroxyl group of the attached glucose for a subsequent glycosyl transfer. Thus, the contrasting active-site architectures suggest that Cluster 8 GTs may recognize different acceptor states, with BAG41686 initiating glycosylation directly on a hydroxymethylated base and AKJ73160 potentially extending an existing DNA-linked glycan.

Having established the potential role of cluster 8 associated with DNA modification, we next asked whether comparable viral GT-associated gene neighborhoods occur across diverse viral genomes. To address this question, we extracted 11 gene window and 15 gene window centered on viral GTs, representing a total 466 genome units, and analyzed them using BGC-Prophet, a deep-learning model for predicting classes of biosynthetic gene clusters. Of the 1,477 evaluated viral GT-centered windows, 511 were classified as Saccharide-associated, comprising 246 15-gene and 265 11-gene windows. To place these findings in a broader biosynthetic context, we carried out a joint embedding analysis of a viral GT-associated loci and reference BGCs from MlBiG database. Leiden clustering identified total 10 global cluster (GC) that well corresponded to annotated biosynthetic product classes, suggesting that the embedding captured chemical difference of BGC classes among reference BGCs (Supplementary Figure 18A). We then calculated cosine similarities between viral and reference BGCs embeddings and selected viral loci for which at least five of ten nearest reference BGCs belonged to the Saccharide class (P@10 ≥ 0.5). 325 positive 15 -gene window results were identified as Saccharide-positive. Together, these observations raise the possibility that viral GTs participate in coordinated biosynthetic modules rather than acting solely as isolated enzymes, potentially contributing to diverse viral glycan structures.

Genomic context adds a different kind of evidence. Cluster 8 is found in more than one genomic setting. Some loci contain hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor and DNA-metabolism genes, while others contain virion-associated and glycan-related genes. Even the DNA-associated loci differ in their predicted precursor routes and arrangement of GT-like proteins. This suggests that related viral enzyme architectures may be deployed in distinct biosynthetic settings, but gene proximity cannot establish a shared product, acceptor or reaction sequence. The B2ZYD6 Type III locus offers the most distinctive chemical hypothesis. Five tandem GT-like genes occur alongside a putative hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor enzyme and proteins associated with sulfate activation and transfer. BAG41679 has an active-site substitution compatible with a uracil-directed precursor route, and the modeled pocket of BAG41686 resembles those of enzymes that glycosylate hydroxymethylated DNA bases directly. In a different Cluster 8 context, AKJ73160 lacks the same base-stacking arrangement and may instead recognize an already glucosylated acceptor. These contrasting pockets suggest possible initiation and extension roles for related GT-like proteins. Recent work has established mono-, di- and trisaccharides on phage DNA, as well as glycosylated 5-hydroxycytosine produced through a distinct precursor route (Pyle et al., 2024; Lee et al., 2026). The distinguishing feature of B2ZYD6 is the proposed coupling of multiple glycosylation steps with sulfate-related chemistry.

Gene-neighborhood heatmap construction.Cluster 3-containing viral neighborhoods were compared using a confidence-weighted gene-class matrix derived from Foldseek annotation outputs. For each candidate locus, neighboring ORFs were structurally searched against PDB100, AFDB-SwissProt, AFDB50, and CATH50, and the resulting named Foldseek hit tables were parsed using a custom rule-based classifier. ORFs were assigned to functional gene classes associated with hydroxymethyl-base precursor formation, pyrimidine/nucleotide metabolism, DNA metabolism, glycan biosynthesis, virion structure, or conserved unknown proteins. Annotation confidence was encoded as a discrete score from 0 to 3 based on Foldseek probability, e-value, query coverage, alignment length, database source, and hit rank. High-confidence hits required probability ≥ 0.90, e-value ≤ 1 × 10⁻⁵, query coverage ≥ 0.50, and alignment length ≥ 100 amino acids; medium-confidence hits required probability ≥ 0.70, e-value ≤ 1 × 10⁻³, query coverage ≥ 0.35, and alignment length ≥ 80 amino acids; weak hits required e-value ≤ 1 × 10⁻² and alignment length ≥ 50 amino acids. CATH-only fold-level hits were capped at medium confidence, and low-ranked hits were penalized to reduce functional overinterpretation.

For each neighborhood, the heatmap value for a given gene class represents the maximum evidence score among all neighboring ORFs assigned to that class, rather than a raw gene count. Generic transferases were not counted as glycosyltransferases unless the annotation specifically supported glycosyltransferase-like function. TET-associated GT-like annotations were also not considered direct evidence of DNA glycosylation; DNA-modification context was inferred from independent neighboring genes such as C5-cytosine methyltransferases, 5mYOX/TET-like dioxygenases, dCMP hydroxymethylases, ThyX/ThyS-like enzymes, or 5hmC/5hmdU-related enzymes. Rows were sorted by inferred neighborhood class and then by DNA-context, glycan-pathway, and virion-structural scores. Heatmaps were plotted in Python using pandas and matplotlib.

Supplementary Fig. 13. Structure-guided annotation of hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine precursor enzymes in DNA-associated cluster 8 loci.Structural and active-site comparison of predicted folate-dependent pyrimidine C5-hydroxymethyltransferases encoded near DNA-associated cluster 8 loci. The top panel shows structural superposition of representative cluster 3-neighborhood enzymes with the crystallographic reference T4 deoxycytidylate 5-hydroxymethyltransferase. The reference structure contains bound tetrahydrofolate (THF) and deoxycytidylate/dCMP-site ligand, providing an active-site template for substrate-recognition analysis. Predicted enzymes from Type I and Type IV loci, including AKJ73159, QFP95377, and QWS69716, preserve the cytosine-directed active-site architecture of T4-like dCMP hydroxymethyltransferases, including the catalytic cysteine, conserved histidine/serine residues, aromatic base-positioning residue, and an Asp residue positioned for cytosine recognition. These features support annotation of these proteins as dCMP C5-hydroxymethyltransferase-like enzymes that can generate 5hmC-type precursors for downstream DNA glycosylation. In contrast, the Type III enzyme BAG41679 preserves the same global fold and catalytic cysteine but contains Asn242 at the position equivalent to the cytosine-specific Asp residue in dCMP-directed enzymes. This Asp-to-Asn active-site substitution is consistent with altered pyrimidine specificity and supports annotation of BAG41679 as a dUMP hydroxymethyltransferase-like enzyme predicted to generate a 5-hydroxymethyluracil-type precursor. Together, these comparisons justify the assignment of Type I/IV loci as 5hmC-linked pathways and the Type III locus as a distinct 5hmdU-linked hydroxymethyl-pyrimidine pathway.
